newsitem.title: USA: Baker calls for stronger U.S. role in Middle East.
newsitem.headline: Baker calls for stronger U.S. role in Middle East.

text.p: Former Secretary of State James Baker called on the U.S. government Thursday to take a stronger role to boost the flagging Middle East peace process and accused it of failing to speak out on Jewish settlements.

Baker, opening a Middle East seminar in Washington, declared himself pessimistic about short and medium-term prospects for peace following the election of the right-wing Likud government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Now that the presidential election in the United States is over it is essential, I think, that the United States assume a stronger leadership role to get the peace process back on track," Baker said.
"Whether the new administration will opt to do that or not is an important question."

Democratic President Bill Clinton, re-elected to a new four-year term last month, decided on Thursday to name U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright as secretary of state to replace Warren Christopher, who retires next month, officials said.

Baker, who helped to convene the landmark Madrid Middle East peace conference in 1991 during the former Republican administration of George Bush, said an effective U.S. policy would involve "the telling of truths that are upsetting."
"This is not a task that has come naturally to the administration in power today here in Washington," he said.

Baker said he was shocked by Christopher's decision, following Netanyahu's election, to tone down U.S. criticism of Jewish settlements in the occupied territories from an "obstacle to peace" to merely a "complicating factor".

"The United States policy on settlements should not be adapted, it shouldn't be changed, if we want peace," he said. "Where are the United States voices today in opposition to increased settlement activity?"
Netanyahu's government has lifted a freeze on expanding settlements imposed by the former Labour government.

"The peace process today in my opinion is at a very, very rough spot in the road and I for one am pessimistic, indeed I'm a little bit depressed, about the prospects for the short to medium term," Baker said.

Israel and the Palestinians have been haggling since October over terms for a partial Israeli troop withdrawal in the West Bank town of Hebron under previous peace accords. Both Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat have said this week they are ready to meet to conclude a deal.
Arafat's chief economic adviser, Mohammed Rashid, told the Washington seminar that "today we are very close to an agreement on Hebron...but we are very far from peace".

He charged that Israel's settlements policy was "killing in advance" three-year negotiations supposed to start this year on issues including the final status of the Palestinian self-rule territories and the future of Jerusalem.
"I am feeling...that we may be nearer to the end of the process than to success," he said.
